topics.kicker: Seat of Congress · Iron dome topped by the Statue of Freedom
topics.briefing: In 1793, George Washington laid the cornerstone of a building meant to look like an ancient Roman temple, with rows of columns and a soaring dome. That dome, rebuilt in cast iron by architect Thomas U. Walter, kept rising even as cannons fired during the Civil War. Today the United States Capitol still holds the Senate and the House of Representatives beneath a bronze Statue of Freedom, high above the National Mall.

tossups.p: In 1954, gunshots fired from the visitors’ gallery by Puerto Rican nationalists wounded five members of Congress meeting inside this building. Architect Benjamin Henry Latrobe, who rebuilt this structure after British troops burned it in 1814, also gave some of its columns distinctive corn-cob-shaped capitals.
tossups.r: Decades later, Thomas U. Walter replaced its wood-and-copper dome with one made of cast iron. For 10 points, name this building in Washington, D.C. that houses the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives.

tossups.p: Workers hoisted the final section of a 19.5-foot bronze figure onto this building’s dome in December 1863, an event marked with a 35-gun salute even as the Civil War still raged. That bronze figure, sculpted by Thomas Crawford and cast with help from an enslaved foundry worker named Philip Reid, depicts an allegorical woman called the Statue of Freedom.
tossups.r: She stands atop a dome that was still under construction during the war, meant to show the Union would endure. For 10 points, name this Washington, D.C. building, home to the Senate and House of Representatives.

tossups.p: Italian-born artist Constantino Brumidi [“broo-MEE-dee”] spent years decorating this building’s hallways with paintings of American plants and animals, in corridors that now bear his name. He also painted a fresco inside this building’s dome canopy showing George Washington rising into the heavens between figures representing Liberty and Victory.
tossups.r: That fresco is called _The Apotheosis of Washington_. For 10 points, name this Washington, D.C. building whose cast-iron dome holds Brumidi’s famous ceiling painting.

tossups.p: A curved, dome-shaped ceiling in this building’s old House chamber reflects sound waves so that a whisper on one side of the room can be clearly heard across the floor on the other side. That chamber, now called National Statuary Hall, displays part of a collection of bronze and marble statues, two donated by each state.
tossups.r: Visitors can test the whispering effect by standing on marked spots on the floor. For 10 points, name this Washington, D.C. building that also houses the Senate.

tossups.p: A physician and self-taught architect named William Thornton won an open design competition held in 1792 to create plans for this building, beating out several trained architects. Pierre L’Enfant had already picked a rise called Jenkins’ Hill as the site for this building, reasoning that the high ground made a fitting spot for the nation’s most important structure.
tossups.r: George Washington laid this building’s cornerstone himself in 1793. For 10 points, name this building, home to the Senate and House of Representatives, located in Washington, D.C.

tossups.p: Even though the United States was consumed by civil war, construction continued on this building’s current dome, a decision President Abraham Lincoln defended as proof the Union would go on. Architect Thomas U. Walter designed that dome, made of cast iron instead of stone, to replace an earlier copper-sheathed wooden dome built decades before by Charles Bulfinch.
tossups.r: The finished cast-iron dome weighs almost nine million pounds. For 10 points, name this Washington, D.C. building.

tossups.p: In the 1850s, this building nearly doubled in length when matching wings for an expanding Senate and House were added under the same architect who later designed its dome. At the center of the older part of this building, a circular room called the Rotunda displays large historical paintings, including John Trumbull’s _Declaration of Independence_ and John Gadsby Chapman’s painting of a Virginia woman’s baptism.
tossups.r: That second painting shows Pocahontas kneeling to take the Christian name Rebecca. For 10 points, name this Washington, D.C. building whose Rotunda hosts lying-in-state ceremonies for deceased leaders.

tossups.p: After American forces lost the Battle of Bladensburg in 1814, British troops marched into Washington and set fire to this building, destroying much of the young nation’s library and legislative records. Rebuilding stretched on for years under several different architects before the structure was fully repaired.
tossups.r: That same week, British troops also burned the White House, at the other end of Pennsylvania Avenue. For 10 points, name this Washington, D.C. building, home to the Senate and House of Representatives.

tossups.p: When this building’s wings were expanded in the 1850s to fit a growing Senate and House, architect Thomas U. Walter designed matching new chambers at either end, nearly doubling the structure’s length. He later capped the whole building with a taller dome made of cast iron instead of stone.
tossups.r: That iron dome weighs almost nine million pounds. For 10 points, name this seat of the U.S. Congress in Washington, D.C.

tossups.p: Deceased presidents and other notable Americans have lain in state beneath this building’s dome, inside a circular room ringed with columns and large historical paintings. On bitterly cold inauguration days, presidents have even taken the oath of office inside that same room instead of on the building’s west front.
tossups.r: This room, called the Rotunda, sits at the heart of a building first planned in the 1790s. For 10 points, name this building in Washington, D.C. that houses Congress.

tossups.p: George Washington himself laid the cornerstone of this building in a ceremony in 1793, though he never lived to see it finished. Inside its dome, Italian immigrant artist Constantino Brumidi later painted a swirling fresco showing Washington rising into the heavens between goddesses representing Liberty and Victory.
tossups.r: That ceiling painting is called _The Apotheosis of Washington_. For 10 points, name this Washington, D.C. building where Congress meets.

tossups.p: This building has survived very different kinds of attacks: British troops set it on fire in 1814, and in 1954 gunmen fired into its House chamber from the visitors’ gallery. After the fire, Congress met for several years in a temporary brick building nearby while this one was rebuilt.
tossups.r: Lawmakers still gather here today beneath a dome topped by the Statue of Freedom. For 10 points, name this seat of the U.S. Congress in Washington, D.C.

tossups.p: An enslaved craftsman named Philip Reid helped cast the bronze statue that crowns this building’s dome, working at a foundry outside Washington during the Civil War. Decades earlier, a physician named William Thornton had beaten out professional competitors to design this building’s original layout.
tossups.r: Construction on Thornton’s design began after George Washington laid the cornerstone in 1793. For 10 points, name this Washington, D.C. building.

tossups.p: Hallways inside this building known as the Brumidi Corridors are covered in painted vines, birds, and insects by the same Italian-born artist who decorated the dome’s ceiling. Later artists kept adding new scenes to those corridors long after Brumidi’s death.
tossups.r: His ceiling fresco inside the dome, _The Apotheosis of Washington_, is even more famous. For 10 points, name this Washington, D.C. building.

tossups.p: A bronze statue of a robed woman called Freedom has stood atop this building’s white dome since 1863. Designed in the Neoclassical style, with rows of columns borrowed from ancient Greek and Roman temples, this building sits at the east end of the National Mall in Washington, D.C.
tossups.r: It is home to both the Senate and the House of Representatives. For 10 points, name this seat of the United States Congress.

trap.title: Capitol or White House?
trap.body: The Capitol and the White House were both set on fire by British troops during the same week in August 1814, so a tossup about either building often mentions the other one burning too. Rushing to answer “White House” as soon as you hear “1814” or “burned” can cost you the game if the rest of the clue is actually describing the Capitol.
trap.fix: Listen for the giveaway: “home to the Senate and House of Representatives” or “Congress meets here” means this building. “Where the president lives and works” means the White House.
trap.line: Real answer line: United States Capitol building.

topics.name: The Night Watch
topics.kicker: Rembrandt’s militia portrait · Famous for dramatic light and shadow
topics.briefing: Rembrandt’s _The Night Watch_ looks like it was painted after dark, but that is just centuries of dirty varnish talking: the scene actually happens in bright daylight. This huge 1642 group portrait shows an Amsterdam militia marching out, led by Captain Frans Banning Cocq, with a mysterious glowing girl and a dead chicken tucked among the soldiers. Visitors can see it for themselves at the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam, where it has survived more than one attack by vandals.

tossups.p: At roughly twelve by fourteen feet, this is the largest painting its artist ever completed, and its full original title describes the militia unit “preparing to march out.” A shield mounted above an arched gateway in the background lists the names of the eighteen men who paid for this work.
tossups.r: Those men belonged to an Amsterdam civic guard unit called the Kloveniers [“kloh-vuh-NEERS”]. For 10 points, name this enormous 1642 group portrait by Rembrandt.

tossups.p: A dead chicken hanging from a girl’s belt in this painting shows off its claws, the heraldic symbol of the Kloveniers, the Amsterdam civic guard unit that commissioned it. Lieutenant Willem van Ruytenburch [“ROY-ten-burkh”], dressed in a lighter uniform, stands beside the militia’s captain near the center of the composition.
tossups.r: That captain, Frans Banning Cocq, wears black clothing and a red sash. For 10 points, name this painting of an armed Dutch militia by Rembrandt.

tossups.p: When this painting was moved to Amsterdam’s town hall in the 1700s, workers trimmed strips from every edge, cutting the most from the left side so the canvas would fit between two columns. That trim sliced off two figures entirely and partially cropped a drummer near the right edge.
tossups.r: Despite the damage, the drummer and a barking dog nearby still appear in the final composition today. For 10 points, name this painting by Rembrandt.

tossups.p: This work belongs to a popular Dutch Golden Age genre called the schutterstuk [“SKHUT-er-stuk”], in which members of a civic militia paid to have themselves painted together. Here, a shield above a stone archway in the background records the names of all eighteen guardsmen who funded the piece.
tossups.r: Unlike most paintings of this type, though, this one shows its subjects caught in motion rather than posed in neat rows. For 10 points, name this dynamic militia portrait by Rembrandt.

tossups.p: Since 2019, museum scientists have used ultra-high-resolution cameras and artificial intelligence to study every centimeter of this painting’s surface inside a glass room in the gallery, letting visitors watch the research happen live. In 1975 and again in 1990, separate attackers damaged the canvas with a knife and then with acid, though conservators repaired it both times.
tossups.r: Those attacks targeted Rembrandt’s most famous surviving work. For 10 points, name this painting at Amsterdam’s Rijksmuseum.

tossups.p: A small girl bathed in golden light appears in the middle of the crowd, even though she was never actually a member of the unit; some historians think she may represent a good-luck mascot or a symbol of the militia’s guild. A dead chicken, claws pointing up, dangles from her belt.
tossups.r: That strange detail refers to the sigil of the Kloveniers, the civic guard group this painting depicts. For 10 points, name this Rembrandt masterpiece.

tossups.p: Besides its two main officers, this painting crowds in at least sixteen other identifiable militiamen, who reportedly paid more for more prominent spots near the front. The lighter-dressed of the two officers, Lieutenant Willem van Ruytenburch, walks just behind and to the side of his captain.
tossups.r: That captain, dressed all in black with a red sash across his chest, is Frans Banning Cocq. For 10 points, identify this painting, Rembrandt’s depiction of an armed Amsterdam militia.

tossups.p: A small dog barks near a drummer on the right side of this painting, startled by the beating of his instrument as the militia prepares to march. That same drummer was nearly lost entirely when the canvas was trimmed down generations after it was painted.
tossups.r: Today the trimmed original hangs in Amsterdam’s Rijksmuseum. For 10 points, name this painting of a Dutch militia, painted by Rembrandt.

tossups.p: Rembrandt completed this painting in 1642, the same year his wife Saskia died, even as commissions like this one were making him one of Amsterdam’s most sought-after painters. The Kloveniers, a civic guard unit armed with matchlock muskets, paid for this group portrait to hang in their guild hall.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this painting that today hangs in the Rijksmuseum, Rembrandt’s dramatic portrait of an armed militia.

tossups.p: A disturbed visitor slashed this painting with a knife in 1975, and in 1990 another attacker sprayed it with acid before guards rinsed the canvas clean with water. Despite that damage, the small girl glowing near the center of the scene, a dead chicken hanging from her belt, remains one of its best-loved details.
tossups.r: She stands out brightly against the painting’s darker, shadowy background. For 10 points, name this Rembrandt work.

tossups.p: Despite its common nickname, the scene in this painting actually takes place in bright daylight; centuries of darkened varnish only made it look like a nighttime scene until later cleaning revealed the truth. Rembrandt built the composition around dramatic contrasts of light and shadow, a technique called chiaroscuro [“kee-AR-oh-SKOO-roh”].
tossups.r: That dramatic lighting highlights a militia captain in black and his lighter-dressed lieutenant. For 10 points, name this painting whose common nickname misleadingly suggests a night scene.

tossups.p: This painting shows an armed civic guard unit gathered beneath a flag and an archway, caught mid-motion as if truly marching out of the frame. It remains the single most famous work by its Dutch artist, who is equally known for his many self-portraits and his Bible scenes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this large 1642 group portrait of a militia, painted by Rembrandt.

tossups.p: Millions of visitors view this painting each year at its home in the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam, where it hangs at the end of a long gallery built to showcase it. It crowds more than two dozen figures around a 17th-century militia company, caught in a burst of motion and shadow.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this huge painting by the Dutch master Rembrandt.

tossups.p: This painting’s dramatic use of light and shadow is one of the clearest examples of its artist’s signature style, called chiaroscuro. Though its nickname suggests a nighttime scene, the militia inside is actually marching out in broad daylight.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this famous group portrait by Rembrandt, housed today in Amsterdam’s Rijksmuseum.

tossups.p: A huge group portrait of an armed Amsterdam militia, painted by Rembrandt in 1642, is the single most famous painting in the Rijksmuseum’s collection. Its subjects stride forward around a captain in black and a glowing girl carrying a dead chicken.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this enormous Dutch militia portrait by Rembrandt.

trap.title: The painter or the painting?
trap.body: Many clues about this work also describe Rembrandt himself, since he painted it, but the required answer is the painting, not the artist. Real answer lines even say to prompt, not fully accept, if a player only names the militia captain, Frans Banning Cocq, since that identifies a person inside the painting rather than the work itself.
trap.fix: Wait for cues like “this painting,” “this group portrait,” or “this work” before you buzz with just the title. If you only remember the captain’s name, buzz anyway and say “Frans Banning Cocq” — you should get a chance to add the title.

topics.kicker: Greek-style memorial on the Mall · Site of MLK’s “I Have a Dream” speech
topics.briefing: Shaped like an ancient Greek temple, the Lincoln Memorial rises at the west end of the National Mall with 36 columns for the 36 states of Lincoln’s time. Inside, Daniel Chester French’s huge marble statue of a seated Abraham Lincoln gazes out over the Reflecting Pool toward the Capitol. Its steps have hosted historic moments far beyond Lincoln’s own era, including Martin Luther King Jr.’s 1963 “I Have a Dream” speech.

tossups.p: Beneath the floor of this memorial sits an unfinished chamber where dripping groundwater has formed small stalactites over the decades; the space is rarely opened to the public. Architect Henry Bacon modeled the exterior of this building partly on the Parthenon in Athens, though he swapped a Greek temple’s usual triangular roofline for a flat one.
tossups.r: Inside, a seated marble statue gazes east across a reflecting pool toward the Washington Monument. For 10 points, name this Greek-style memorial on the National Mall.

tossups.p: Congress created a commission in 1911 to plan this structure, choosing a swampy site near the Potomac over a location some lawmakers favored near Union Station. Construction began in 1914 and finished in 1922, when former president William Howard Taft, who had chaired the planning commission, presided over its dedication.
tossups.r: The ceremony came nearly sixty years after the death of the man honored inside. For 10 points, name this memorial to Abraham Lincoln.

tossups.p: The same sculptor who designed this memorial’s centerpiece also created _The Minute Man_ statue in Concord, Massachusetts. That centerpiece, carved from white Georgia marble by the Piccirilli [“pih-chih-RIL-ee”] Brothers’ studio in New York, stands roughly nineteen feet tall even though it depicts its subject only seated, not standing.
tossups.r: Sculptor Daniel Chester French originally planned a statue about half that size. For 10 points, name this Greek-temple-style memorial on the National Mall.

tossups.p: Daniel Chester French originally sketched a statue about ten feet tall for the center of this memorial, but enlarged his design to roughly nineteen feet after realizing a smaller figure would look lost in such a large room. Sculptors carved the statue’s two hands differently: one is loosely open, and the other is clenched into a fist.
tossups.r: Visitors sometimes read those two hands as symbols of both strength and compassion. For 10 points, name this memorial honoring the 16th president.

tossups.p: Builders deliberately used stone quarried from many different states for this memorial, including limestone for its walls and marble from Tennessee and Alabama, as a symbol of national unity after a war that had divided the country. Thirty-six fluted Doric columns ring the outside, one for each state in the Union at the time of the honoree’s death.
tossups.r: Those columns support a flat roof rather than the triangular pediment of a typical Greek temple. For 10 points, name this memorial on the National Mall.

tossups.p: Carved into the attic wall above this memorial’s colonnade are the names of the 48 states that existed when it was dedicated in 1922. When Alaska and Hawaii later joined the Union, there was no room left up top, so their names were added on a separate plaque near the entrance instead.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Greek-style memorial honoring the 16th president on the National Mall.

tossups.p: The full texts of two of its honoree’s most famous speeches are carved into this memorial’s interior walls, each beneath a mural painted by Jules Guerin [“zhool geh-RAN”] showing symbolic figures representing themes like Unity and Emancipation. One speech, delivered at a Pennsylvania battlefield, begins “Four score and seven years ago.”
tossups.r: The other inscribed text is his Second Inaugural Address. For 10 points, name this memorial whose seated statue overlooks both speeches.

tossups.p: In 1939, after she was barred from performing at a nearby concert hall because she was Black, singer Marian Anderson instead gave an open-air concert on the steps of this memorial to a crowd of 75,000 people. Secretary of the Interior Harold Ickes and First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt helped arrange the historic performance.
tossups.r: Those same steps later hosted an even larger crowd in 1963. For 10 points, name this memorial where Martin Luther King Jr. gave his “I Have a Dream” speech.

tossups.p: From its elevated platform, this memorial’s statue gazes east across a long reflecting pool toward the Washington Monument and the dome of the Capitol in the distance. Its 36 exterior columns are made of Colorado Yule marble, while the interior floor uses pink Tennessee marble.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Greek Doric-style memorial to the 16th president, located on the National Mall.

tossups.p: This building’s image has appeared on the back of the U.S. five-dollar bill for decades, and from 1959 until a 2009 redesign, a tiny version of it also decorated the reverse side of the one-cent coin. Robert Todd Lincoln, the only surviving son of the man honored here, attended its dedication ceremony in 1922.
tossups.r: Its 36 exterior columns represent the states in the Union at the time of its honoree’s death. For 10 points, name this Greek-style memorial on the National Mall.

tossups.p: Modeled loosely on an ancient Greek temple, this building has no front door in the traditional sense; visitors instead climb a wide set of steps to reach an open colonnade. Inside sits a single enormous marble statue, designed by Daniel Chester French, of a seated man resting his hands on the arms of a chair.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this memorial to the 16th U.S. president, located at the west end of the National Mall.

tossups.p: Park rangers occasionally lead rare tours into an unfinished basement-level space beneath this memorial, where support columns rise among small mineral formations that have grown since construction. Above that hidden chamber, a massive seated statue has watched over the National Mall since 1922.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this memorial to Abraham Lincoln, built in the style of a Greek temple.

tossups.p: Thirty-six Doric columns circle this building, each representing a state in the Union at the time of the Civil War president’s death. A reflecting pool stretches out in front of it toward a tall stone obelisk.
tossups.r: Inside, a giant marble statue of Abraham Lincoln sits facing east. For 10 points, name this memorial on the National Mall.

tossups.p: Crowds have gathered on the steps of this memorial for historic moments far beyond its original dedication, including Marian Anderson’s 1939 concert and Martin Luther King Jr.’s 1963 speech about a dream. A seated statue of its honoree watches over both the steps and the National Mall beyond.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Greek-style memorial to the 16th president.

tossups.p: A huge seated statue of Abraham Lincoln, designed by Daniel Chester French, sits inside this Greek-temple-style building at the west end of the National Mall in Washington, D.C. Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his “I Have a Dream” speech from its steps in 1963.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this memorial honoring the 16th president.

topics.briefing: French sculptor Auguste Rodin spent 37 years working on a single pair of bronze doors and never considered them finished. Commissioned for a museum that was never built, the doors crowd more than 180 wrestling, falling figures drawn from Dante’s _Inferno_ onto one six-meter-tall frame. Rodin kept enlarging his favorite figures into famous statues of their own, including the brooding man now known as _The Thinker_ — itself a separate answer line, so don’t mix them up.

trap.title: Doorway or The Thinker?
trap.body: _The Gates of Hell_ contains dozens of embedded figures, including _The Thinker_, _The Three Shades_, and _Ugolino and His Sons_; even _The Kiss_ began as part of it. Several real tossups whose actual answer is “_The Thinker_” prompt on “_The Gates of Hell_” because their early clues — a museum commission, an assistant who enlarged it, its original title _The Poet_ — describe only the smaller statue, not the whole bronze doorway.

topics.kicker: Leonardo’s mural of Jesus’s final meal · A landmark of linear perspective
topics.briefing: In a Milan monastery’s dining hall, Leonardo da Vinci painted thirteen men sharing a meal, freezing the exact moment Jesus announces that one of them will betray him. Leonardo used a risky paint recipe instead of true fresco, so the mural began flaking within his own lifetime. It still survived a doorway cut through its bottom edge, soldiers stabling horses in the room, and a World War II bombing raid that wrecked the room around it.

tossups.p: This work’s apostles sit in four groups of three, each group reacting differently to a sudden announcement. Three windows behind the central figure’s head align with the room’s real architecture so every perspective line in the room meets at his right temple.
tossups.r: A doorway cut into the wall in 1652 later sliced off the painted feet of the central figure. For 10 points, name this mural by Leonardo da Vinci showing Jesus and his Twelve Apostles.

tossups.p: Thomas raises his index finger beside the central figure in this work, a gesture some read as foreshadowing his later doubt. A disembodied hand, believed to belong to Peter, holds a knife pointed away from the table.
tossups.r: The betrayer among the diners sits in shadow clutching a bag of silver coins near a knocked-over salt cellar. For 10 points, name this painting of Jesus’s final meal, found in a Milan monastery.

tossups.p: French revolutionary troops stabled horses in the room containing this work in 1796 and scratched at the painted eyes of its figures. A flood around 1800 left roughly two feet of water in that same room, according to the writer Goethe [“GUR-tuh”].
tossups.r: A pupil named Giampietrino [“jahm-pyeh-TREE-no”] painted a nearly full-size copy that later guided restorers. For 10 points, name this mural depicting Jesus’s last meal with his disciples, painted by Leonardo da Vinci.

tossups.p: An 1821 restoration attempt by Stefano Barezzi [“bah-RETZ-ee”], who tried to peel the plaster off in sections, damaged this work further. It faces a Crucifixion fresco by Giovanni Donato da Montorfano [“mohn-tor-FAH-no”] on the opposite wall of the same room.
tossups.r: Sandbags protected it when Allied bombing destroyed the room’s roof in 1943. For 10 points, name this painting of the Twelve Apostles’ final meal with Jesus, located in Milan’s Santa Maria delle Grazie.

tossups.p: Three lunette arches above this work display the coat of arms of the Sforza [“SFORT-sah”] family, who ruled Milan when it was painted. On the far right, the apostles Matthew, Jude Thaddeus, and Simon the Zealot lean together, gesturing back toward the center.
tossups.r: It was painted in tempera on dry plaster rather than true fresco, which caused the paint to begin flaking within years. For 10 points, name this mural of Jesus’s final meal, by Leonardo da Vinci.

tossups.p: In this work, the youthful, androgynous-looking apostle seated to the central figure’s right has sometimes been mistaken by modern novelists for Mary Magdalene, though art historians agree the figure is John. John and Peter lean toward each other in surprise while the betrayer, seated in their same group, leans away.
tossups.r: A copy by one of the artist’s pupils later helped guide its twentieth-century restoration. For 10 points, name this painting showing Jesus’s last meal with his Twelve Apostles.

tossups.p: This work is sometimes contrasted with a version of the same Biblical scene by Paolo Veronese [“veh-roh-NEH-zeh”], which was renamed to refer to the House of Levi after Church officials accused Veronese of indecorum. The painter Tintoretto [“tin-toh-RET-toh”] later depicted the same scene from a dramatic diagonal angle.
tossups.r: Unlike those two versions, this one was painted directly onto a monastery dining-hall wall in Milan. For 10 points, name this depiction of Jesus’s final meal with his apostles, by Leonardo da Vinci.

tossups.p: A twenty-one-year restoration of this work, completed in 1999 and led by Pinin Brambilla Barcilon [“bar-chee-LOHN”], sparked controversy among art historians over how dramatically its colors changed. The mural covers an entire end wall roughly fifteen feet tall and almost twenty-nine feet wide.
tossups.r: Visitors today must reserve tickets and are given only fifteen minutes inside the climate-controlled room to view it. For 10 points, name this Leonardo da Vinci mural of the Twelve Apostles’ final meal with Jesus.

tossups.p: This work was commissioned by Ludovico Sforza, the Duke of Milan, as part of renovations to a Dominican monastery. In it, one apostle tips over a salt cellar, a detail many read as foreshadowing betrayal.
tossups.r: That apostle, Judas, sits in shadow clutching a small bag of silver coins. For 10 points, name this mural depicting the moment Jesus announces that one of his Twelve Apostles will betray him.

tossups.p: In this painting, every orthogonal line of the ceiling and side walls converges on a single point at the central figure’s temple, a triumph of linear perspective. The room it occupies also contains a Crucifixion scene by Montorfano on the facing wall.
tossups.r: A doorway later carved through its base removed the central figure’s painted feet. For 10 points, name this mural of Jesus’s last meal with his twelve disciples, found in Milan, Italy.

tossups.p: This work’s original plaster surface began flaking apart within years, since its creator rejected true fresco for a tempera recipe that let him revise his work slowly. By 1556, the writer Giorgio Vasari already described it as a faded “muddle of blots.”
tossups.r: Despite the damage, its composition of thirteen men around a table remains instantly recognizable. For 10 points, name this painting of Jesus’s final meal, by Leonardo da Vinci.

tossups.p: A copy of this work by the painter Giampietrino, now in London, preserved details that had worn away from the original by the twentieth century. Three windows glow behind the central figure, softly framing his head like a halo.
tossups.r: It depicts thirteen men seated behind a long table on the day before a crucifixion. For 10 points, name this mural of Jesus and his Twelve Apostles sharing a final meal, painted on a Milan monastery wall.

tossups.p: Rather than painting on wet plaster, this work’s creator used a mixture including tempera and oil on dry plaster, trading durability for the ability to work slowly and add fine detail. Three coats of arms belonging to the ruling Sforza family top this work, while a doorway later cut away part of its lower edge.
tossups.r: It depicts the dramatic moment after Jesus tells his disciples that one of them will betray him. For 10 points, name this Leonardo da Vinci mural of the Twelve Apostles’ final meal.

tossups.p: This work’s central figure spreads his hands calmly over the table while the twelve men flanking him erupt into shock, anger, and confusion at his words. One figure beside him raises an index finger, while another, in shadow just left of center, clutches a small bag and leans away into darkness.
tossups.r: Milan’s Santa Maria delle Grazie has housed this mural since the 1490s. For 10 points, name this depiction of Jesus’s last meal with his disciples, painted by Leonardo da Vinci.

tossups.p: Painted for a Dominican monastery’s dining hall, this work shows twelve apostles divided into four groups of three around a central figure, all on one side of a long table. A hidden hand near one edge of the table holds a knife, pointed away from the group, said to belong to the apostle Peter.
tossups.r: Napoleonic troops later used the room housing it as a stable and threw stones at its painted faces. For 10 points, name this Leonardo da Vinci mural depicting Jesus’s final meal with his Twelve Apostles.
